title: Edmund and the Hymn
premise: Folklorist Oscar Iversen arrives in the remote village of Hallowmere to record a funeral hymn that locals will sing only once, never twice, and she dismisses their fear as superstition. But the hymn is a covenant: each full performance feeds something beneath the village, and her recordings have begun completing it, while every mirror in her rented house lags one second behind reality—the thing below learning to imitate her. As villagers who once sang for her start dying with hymn-verse words carved into their skin, Oscar discovers the song's lost final verse can either seal the entity away or free it, depending on who sings it. In the flooded chapel where the hymn was born, Oscar must perform the last verse alone—refusing to sing along with her own reflection—and by giving up her recorded voice, and with it the identity she built as an observer, she seals the thing below at the cost of being forgotten by everyone she ever documented.
about_author: Gideon Whitlock is the pen name of a former church organist from coastal Maine who spent a decade transcribing dying musical traditions in isolated communities before turning to horror. His work is known for its scholarly dread, treating folklore not as decoration but as a living contract with terrible fine print.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Oscar Iversen arrives in Hallowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing elderly residents about the Hollow Hymn sung only at funerals, never repeated. The vicar, Edith Marsh, refuses her flatly; a dying woman, Agnes Pike, agrees to hum four bars if Oscar leaves immediately after. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: confident curiosity curdling into unease when Agnes whispers 'don't learn it all.'

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Oscar catalogs her recordings in the rented Hollis farmhouse and notices her reflection in the hallway mirror moves a fraction late—a blink arriving after her own. She blames fatigue, but the lag grows measurable: one full second. A neighbor, Tom Brack, sees her mirror and goes pale, telling her to cover them all. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: rational denial cracking under empirical evidence she cannot explain.

chapters.title: What the Tape Remembers
chapters.summary: Playing back Agnes's humming, Oscar hears a second voice underneath—low, wet, harmonizing a verse Agnes never sang. She interviews Tom, who reveals his grandfather helped bury the hymn's composer in the flooded chapel in 1911 after 'the singing year,' when eleven villagers drowned themselves mid-verse. POV: Oscar with a brief Edith interlude. Emotional beat: dread replacing skepticism as folklore becomes testimony.

chapters.title: The Congregation of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Oscar finds parish records: every generation, someone transcribes or records the hymn, and within weeks the whole choir of that season dies, each found with lyrics scored into their flesh. The last folklorist, in 1974, vanished leaving tapes identical to hers. Her mirrors now show the room continuing without her when she steps away. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as she realizes she was invited, not incidental.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: Vicar Edith Marsh admits the village has always known: the hymn isn't worship but containment, sung once per death to renew a bargain made with something in the water below the chapel. Oscar's recordings are nearly a complete performance—the entity needs only the final verse, which no living person knows. Edith begs her to burn the tapes. POV: Edith, then Oscar. Emotional beat: guilt and fury—Oscar realizes her scholarship has been a weapon aimed at her.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Refusing to destroy her life's work, Oscar instead studies the tapes, reconstructing the hymn's structure and finding the final verse deliberately excised from every source—cut out like a tumor. The lag in her mirrors spreads to windows and still water; her reflection now mouths words slightly out of sync, practicing something. Tom dies at the mill pond, verses carved down his arms. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: obsession overtaking fear—she must know the ending.

chapters.title: The Composer's Daughter
chapters.summary: In the archive of a shuttered asylum, Oscar finds the composer's daughter, institutionalized in 1912, alive at 118 and mute—until she sees Oscar's recorder and writes one line: the opening of the final verse, then 'it must be given, not taken.' That night every mirror in Hallowmere reflects the flooded chapel instead of the rooms they hang in. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: horrified awe—the last witness has been waiting a century for someone to come.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: The village floods from below; wells run backward, and the drowned of 1911 stand in the shallows singing the first five verses in perfect unison, waiting for a sixth voice. Edith drowns leading them away from the schoolhouse, buying Oscar a night. The entity speaks through Oscar's own recordings, offering her a bargain: finish the hymn together and survive, remembered forever. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: temptation at its most seductive—survival dressed as love.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Oscar wades into the flooded chapel where the composer's bones rest on the altar, plays nothing, and sings the final verse from memory—alone, refusing to harmonize with her lagging reflection, which screams and mimics and fails. The verse is a renunciation: the singer gives up her voice, her name, her place in every record. The water closes over the entity mid-note. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: climax of sacrifice—love for truth surrendered to duty to the living.

chapters.title: Unrecorded
chapters.summary: Weeks later, a quiet woman no one in Hallowmere recognizes helps rebuild the village; her tapes play static, her field notes bear no name, and archives worldwide list her contributions as anonymous. Only the composer's daughter, now dead, left one final written line addressed to her: 'Some songs cost the singer everything, and that is why they work.' The mirrors show rooms exactly on time. POV: close third on the unnamed woman. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution—identity traded for survival, meaning preserved only in what cannot be proven.
